title: Persistence Detection

theory.concept: Persistence is anything that returns execution to the attacker after a reboot or a logoff. Windows offers dozens of mechanisms: Run and RunOnce keys, scheduled tasks, services, WMI event subscriptions, startup folders, DLL search-order hijacking, image file execution options, and accounts. Linux offers cron, systemd units and timers, rc scripts, shell profiles and SSH authorized_keys.
theory.why: Eradication fails if one mechanism survives. Attackers deliberately plant several of different types, expecting the obvious one to be found.
look: Scheduled tasks whose action is a script interpreter or a binary in a user-writable path
Services created with a random or system-imitating name pointing outside System32
WMI __EventFilter and CommandLineEventConsumer pairs - stealthy and frequently missed
New SSH keys in authorized_keys, new systemd units, modified shell profiles
Anything created during the confirmed attack window
fp: Vendor software legitimately creates tasks, services and Run entries constantly
Group Policy deploys scheduled tasks estate-wide
tips: Enumerate by creation time, not by suspicion. Everything created during the attack window deserves a look.
WMI subscription persistence is invisible to a casual look at autoruns - check it explicitly.

case.alert: Persistence hunt across confirmed compromised hosts
case.brief: Enumerate every persistence mechanism the intruder established across the three confirmed hosts. Missing one means the eradication fails and the operator returns.

hints: Sort every artefact by creation date and ignore everything that predates 2026-03-04. The attack window does the filtering for you.
Each host has two mechanisms, not one. On SRV-FILE02 the second one is a pair of WMI objects that only make sense together.
review: Six mechanisms, deliberately varied so that finding one does not reveal the rest: on WKS-2041 the HKCU Run value and a scheduled task that re-downloads a script from the C2 daily at 07:00; on SRV-FILE02 an auto-start service (7045, unsigned binary in ProgramData) plus a WMI __EventFilter and CommandLineEventConsumer pair, which is the one most teams miss because it does not appear in normal startup locations; on SRV-LNX-04 the ten-minute cron and a second SSH key added at 07:49 with the misleading comment root@localhost. The OneDrive Run entry, the UpdateOrchestrator task, the Veeam service and the 2024 CI key are legitimate. Removal must be coordinated - clean one host while the others still beacon and the operator simply redeploys.
next: Persistence is mapped. Now account for the identities: the operator has been using more than one set of credentials, and at least one user account is behaving in ways its owner cannot explain.

title: Account Compromise

theory.concept: Account compromise investigation compares observed identity behaviour against a behavioural baseline: where the account normally authenticates from, at what hours, to what resources, and with what device. Cloud identity platforms add session, device and MFA telemetry. Key anomalies are impossible travel, MFA fatigue, new device registration and session token reuse.
theory.why: Once credentials are valid, nothing looks like an exploit. Identity telemetry is often the only place the intrusion is visible.
look: Sign-ins from an ASN or country the user has never used, especially within an impossible interval of a legitimate one
Repeated MFA prompts followed by one approval - push-bombing
New MFA method or device registered by the user shortly after a suspicious sign-in
Mailbox rules created to auto-delete or forward - a standard post-compromise move
Legacy authentication protocols that bypass MFA entirely
fp: VPNs, mobile roaming and cloud gateways produce genuine geo anomalies
Users do travel - check the calendar and the ticket queue before declaring impossible travel
tips: Check for a new MFA method registration. If the attacker registers their own, a password reset alone will not evict them.
Mailbox rule creation is one of the highest-fidelity business-email-compromise indicators.

hints: Read the sign-in log as a sequence of attempts rather than individual events. What changed between the fifth attempt and the sixth, and what did the attacker do immediately after getting in?
Two actions after the successful sign-in are designed to outlast your response: one keeps the attacker's access, the other keeps the user from noticing. Find both.
review: Classic cloud account takeover. Five MFA pushes at roughly 45-second intervals at 03:40 local time until the user approved one to stop the noise, then immediate registration of the attacker's own authenticator device (SM-A125) - which is why a password reset alone would not evict them. An inbox rule was created to move any mail mentioning invoice, payment, bank, IT or security into RSS Subscriptions and mark it read, concealing both fraud replies and security warnings. 592 mail items were accessed across the inbox, sent items and Finance Approvals, followed by a fraudulent remittance-details email to a genuine partner - business email compromise. The 01:12 access needed no MFA because the session token was already valid, which is why token revocation must accompany the reset. The morning sign-in from her own device is the real user.
next: The attacker holds a finance identity and a foothold on three hosts. The next question is whether they have gained administrative rights anywhere they should not have them.

title: Privilege Escalation Detection

theory.concept: Privilege escalation moves an attacker from the rights they have to the rights they want. On Windows the common routes are credential theft from memory, abusing over-permissive service or scheduled task configurations, unquoted service paths, token impersonation, exploiting a vulnerable driver, and simply adding an account to a privileged group. On Linux: sudo misconfiguration, SUID binaries, writable service units and kernel exploits.
theory.why: Escalation is the hinge of an intrusion. Before it, damage is bounded by one user's rights; after it, the attacker owns the estate.
look: 4672 (special privileges assigned) for accounts that should never have them
4732/4728 group membership additions outside change control
Service binary paths or permissions modified by a non-admin account
Token manipulation: a process running with higher integrity than its parent
Linux: new SUID binaries, sudoers edits, unexpected 'USER=root' sudo entries
fp: Administrators legitimately trigger 4672 every time they log on
Installers modify service configurations as part of normal upgrades
tips: Compare integrity level between parent and child - Medium spawning High without a UAC prompt is a finding.
A group membership change is a five-second action with permanent consequences; audit it hourly during an incident.

hints: Escalation here required no exploit at all. Follow the sequence: query a service, check whether its folder is writable, replace the binary, wait for a restart.
The proof of escalation is a single field changing value between two events on the same code. Find the field that reads Medium in one place and System in another.
review: No exploit was needed. nwsync.exe, running as m.chen at Medium integrity, queried BackupMgrSvc, found that BUILTIN\Users held modify rights on its program directory - a 2021 vendor installation defect that was never remediated - replaced the signed service binary with its own, and waited for the scheduled restart. At 09:43:02 the same code was running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, launched by services.exe. From there it read LSASS memory (unsigned binary, no ticket, no admin account - the exact opposite of the SRV-APP03 false positive), enumerated Domain Admins, and installed the NWSyncSvc persistence service. By 10:18 svc_backup2, the backdoor domain account from the DC-01 case, was exercising SeDebugPrivilege on this host: the two intrusion paths have converged. Every credential cached on this server must now be treated as stolen.
next: With SYSTEM on a file server and a Domain Admin backdoor, the operator can move anywhere. Track their movement between hosts.

title: Lateral Movement Detection

theory.concept: Lateral movement is authenticated access from one host to another using stolen credentials. The common methods each leave a recognisable signature: remote service creation (PsExec: 7045 plus admin share access), WMI and WinRM execution, RDP (Type 10 logons), scheduled task creation on a remote host, and pass-the-hash producing NTLM network logons without a preceding Kerberos ticket request.
theory.why: Movement is where a contained incident becomes an estate-wide one. Detecting it early limits how much has to be rebuilt.
look: 4648 - logon with explicitly supplied credentials, the classic runas/lateral indicator
4624 Type 3 with NTLM where the environment is otherwise Kerberos
7045 service installed with a random-looking name, or a binary in ADMIN$
5140/5145 access to ADMIN$, C$ and IPC$ shares
Sequences of the same account authenticating to many hosts in a short window
fp: Administrative tooling, patch deployment and monitoring all authenticate widely by design
Backup agents access administrative shares routinely
tips: Build the movement graph: source host, destination host, account, method, time. That graph is the containment plan.
Count distinct destinations per account in an hour - humans and scripts have very different shapes.

case.alert: Remote service creation and administrative share access across multiple hosts
case.brief: Map the attacker's movement through the estate: which accounts, which methods, which destinations, and identify the one host where movement was attempted but failed.

mitre: T1021.002 SMB/Admin Shares / T1569.002 Service Execution / T1021.001 RDP

On the domain controller at 11:03:40 they exercised DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All, which is DCSync: the attacker can now replicate password hashes for every account in the domain, including krbtgt. That is a full domain compromise and a double krbtgt reset is required. SRV-PCI01 refused them twice with 0xC000015B - not a wrong password, but 'logon type not granted', because the segmented cardholder environment denies network logon to non-PCI accounts. That single control is the only thing that kept the PCI scope out of the incident, and it belongs in the report as the one defence that worked. The svc_sccm activity is daily patch deployment.
next: The operator now has directory-level control and three beaconing implants. Characterise their command-and-control infrastructure in full before the block list goes to the network team.

title: Command & Control

theory.concept: C2 is the channel between implant and operator. Analysts classify it by transport (HTTP/S, DNS, SMB named pipes, cloud services), by cadence (fixed interval, jitter, long sleep) and by architecture (direct, redirector, domain fronting, peer-to-peer through an internal pivot). Modern frameworks randomise timing and blend into normal traffic, so detection leans on aggregation over time.
theory.why: Blocking one address rarely ends the intrusion. Mapping every channel, including internal pivots, is what makes the block effective.
look: Regular intervals once jitter is averaged out; compute the mean and the variance
Consistent small payload sizes in both directions
Long sleep implants that only wake every few hours - easy to miss on a one-hour view
Internal hosts relaying for hosts that have no direct internet path (SMB pipe or HTTP proxy pivot)
Repeated TLS fingerprints (JA3) or certificate serials across unrelated destinations
fp: Monitoring agents, update services and chat clients all beacon legitimately
Cloud-hosted C2 shares addresses with legitimate services - block by domain and fingerprint, not only by IP
tips: Average the intervals rather than eyeballing them; jitter is designed to defeat eyeballing.
Ask how every compromised host reaches the internet. A host with no route must be pivoting through one that has.

case.alert: Full C2 channel characterisation prior to coordinated block
case.brief: Map every command-and-control channel in use, including any internal relay. The network team executes your block list in one action - anything you miss keeps the operator connected.

mitre: T1071.001 Web Protocols / T1071.004 DNS / T1090.001 Internal Proxy / T1573 Encrypted Channel

review: Four distinct channels. Blocking the external IP alone would leave the long-sleep channel, the DNS tunnel and the internal relay intact - which is why containment must be simultaneous.

title: Data Exfiltration Detection

theory.concept: Exfiltration normally has three phases: collection (finding and reading the data), staging (compressing and often encrypting it into an archive, frequently in a temp or public directory), and transfer (over C2, DNS, cloud storage, email or removable media). Each phase leaves different evidence, and the staging archive is usually the best single artefact for quantifying impact.
theory.why: Impact assessment, regulatory notification and negotiation posture all depend on what actually left, not what could have.
look: Archive creation (.7z, .zip, .rar) in %TEMP%, %PROGRAMDATA% or /tmp containing business documents
Volume asymmetry outbound, or sustained small transfers over DNS
Uploads to personal cloud storage from servers
File access counts far above a user's baseline
Deleted staging archives shortly after a transfer completes
fp: Backup, DR replication and legitimate cloud migration produce enormous outbound volumes
Analytics and reporting jobs read thousands of files by design
tips: Convert DNS tunnel volume to bytes: labels carry a limited payload per query, so queries times payload gives a credible estimate.
Record file counts and classifications; the privacy and legal teams need them, not a description of the traffic.

review: Collection: 214 payroll spreadsheets (186 MB) and 1,102 contract PDFs (1.4 GB) read as SYSTEM; the HR personnel share refused access, so those records are out of scope - a detail the privacy officer needs stated explicitly. Staging: three password-protected 7-Zip archives in C:\ProgramData\cache totalling roughly 344 MB, with the password visible in the command line, so contents can be confirmed. Transfer: the DNS tunnel moved 5,652 queries at 180 bytes, about 1 MB in total - far too little for 344 MB, which proves the bulk went out over the HTTPS C2 channel and makes the DNS tunnel a low-bandwidth control and overflow path rather than the main route. Archive d3 is the worst of it: harvested credentials and an Active Directory database dump. The archives were deleted at 23:58 to frustrate forensics but were recovered from volume shadow copies. Scope for notification is 1,840 employees.
next: You have the full technical picture on four hosts. Now it must be reproduced as a correlated investigation inside the SIEM, using query syntax rather than curated evidence panels - the way it would be done on a real console.

title: SIEM Investigation

theory.concept: A SIEM normalises logs from many sources into common fields and lets the analyst search, filter, aggregate and correlate across them. The workflow is always the same: scope a time window, filter to relevant sources, pivot on an entity (IP, user, host, hash), aggregate to spot outliers, then correlate across sources to build the sequence.
theory.why: Curated evidence panels do not exist in real life. The analyst has to build the picture with queries.
look: Field names and their normalised equivalents: src_ip, dest_ip, user, host, event_id, process
Aggregations: count by source, distinct destinations per account, events per minute
Time windows that include enough before-and-after context to establish baseline
Correlation across sources: authentication plus process plus network for the same entity
fp: A correlation rule joining on a shared field can produce spurious matches - verify the underlying events
Timezone mismatches between sources create false sequences; normalise to UTC
tips: Pivot on entities, not on alerts. One IP searched across every index beats ten alert reviews.
Always state the time window in your findings; a count without a window is meaningless.

review: Fifteen failed logons from 203.0.113.55 (twelve against svc_backup, three during username enumeration). svc_backup2 authenticated to four distinct hosts, installed services on two, accessed shares on three, and performed one directory replication - the DCSync. SRV-FILE02's 5,698 network events dwarf the others because of the DNS tunnel query volume, not because it beacons more often. Two results are noise: WKS-2011 is a parent-process normalisation error (the real parent was ccmexec.exe) and SRV-APP03 is the authorised admin session under INC-20449. Every count here is only meaningful with its window attached, which is why the window is part of the finding, not a footnote.

title: Detection Engineering

theory.concept: Detection engineering turns incident knowledge into durable rules. A good detection has a clear hypothesis, precise logic, a stated data source requirement, known false positives with documented exceptions, a severity, and a response action. Detections are ranked by durability: hashes and IPs are trivially changed, tool artefacts and infrastructure are harder to change, and behaviours are hardest of all.
theory.why: An incident that produces no detections will recur. Rules are the only output of an investigation that keeps working after everyone goes home.
look: Which observed artefact is cheapest for the attacker to change, and which is most expensive
Whether the data source required by the rule is actually collected estate-wide
Expected false positive volume and the exception that handles it without blinding the rule
A response action a Tier-1 analyst can execute without further interpretation
fp: Rules written narrowly around one incident break on the next variant
Rules written broadly generate volume nobody triages, which is worse than no rule
tips: Test every candidate rule against historical data before deploying it; count how many hits the last 30 days would have produced.
Write the exception as a condition in the rule, not as a note asking analysts to remember something.

case.alert: Post-incident detection development for TA-4411 tradecraft
case.brief: Select and evaluate detection candidates from the incident. Each candidate has been backtested against 30 days of historical data - use those results to decide what ships, what needs tuning, and what must be rejected.

recommend.text: Ship D2, D3 (with an analytics-domain exception), D5, D6 (with vendor-agent exceptions), D7 (with a mail-appliance exception) and D8; reject D4; retire D1 and D9 to low-confidence enrichment; and raise Linux auditd coverage as a priority gap.

hints: Rank every candidate on two axes: how much noise it generates and how cheaply the attacker can evade it. Rules that score badly on both are the easy rejects.
A false positive is not automatically disqualifying. Ask whether you can name its cause precisely enough to write it into the rule as a condition.
review: D4 is rejected: 4,218 hits with essentially all of them benign is a rule that guarantees a missed real alert. D1 and D9 are demonstrably low durability - the actor rebuilt the binary within hours, which is exactly why the hash rule missed SRV-FILE02, and a single IP rotates in minutes; both become enrichment rather than detections. D2 ships and is the strongest rule here because it caught the rebuilt variant, though it is blind on Linux where EDR coverage is zero. D3, D6 and D7 ship with named exceptions written into the logic rather than left as analyst folklore. D8 ships despite a 2-in-3 false positive rate because three alerts a month is trivial and a missed Domain Admins addition is catastrophic - false positive rate must always be weighed against consequence. D5 is the most valuable strategically: it fires on the initial .lnk execution, before any persistence or C2, which would have cut this entire incident at minute one. The Linux auditd gap at 40 percent is the coverage finding, and the intrusion started on Linux.
